extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics instructors, mathematics-education researchers, and curriculum developers
extracted.subtask_description: Identify, categorize, and tally common writing errors in expository (procedural/explanatory) mathematics writing produced by college students; provide guidance/examples for each error type. The rubric is used to assess clarity, correctness, and communicative quality of students' mathematical explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of Mathematical Terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct use of mathematical terms is very important when doing expository writing. Mathematics requires a very precise use of language. Misuse of a mathematical term, if not corrected, will create confusion among the reader of the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: saying or writing “the limit converges” (misuse of ‘limit’), or using the word “equation” to mean a mathematical expression that is not an equation. Check that definitions are understood and applied correctly; avoid using technical terms inappropriately. (In the study this error was coded MMT and tallied.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of Mathematical Symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, symbols are integral components of communication and thus must be used appropriately. Part of being able to write well in mathematics is to know when to use symbols or when to use words instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common mistakes: misuse of the equal sign (using “=” to join lines that are not equal), using material-implication or other logical symbols to mean equality, and treating upper-/lower-case letters interchangeably. Guidance: ensure each symbol is used with its conventional meaning; prefer words when a symbol would obscure meaning; remember mathematics is case-sensitive. (Coded MMS in the study; counts were tallied.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorrect Notations
rubrics_metrics.description: Notations in mathematics are the symbolic expressions which have precise and established meaning. Using different notations interchangeably may confuse readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: confusing {a_n} (a sequence) with a_n (a term of a sequence). Verify that specific notations are used consistently and conform to standard conventions for the subfield. (Coded IN; the study recorded relatively few of these errors.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorrect Grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: Good quality writing observes correct grammar. Standard grammatical rules apply in mathematics writing: sentences, subject-verb agreement, correct phrase/sentence distinctions, spelling, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: subject-verb agreement errors ("Since the limit exist..."), mistaking a phrase for a sentence ("Since/is a function"). Many mathematicians insist on complete sentences; grammar affects clarity and professionalism. (Coded IG; this was the most frequent error and was tallied per occurrence.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorrect Capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalization errors include capitalizing words which should not be capitalized and failing to capitalize words that should be capitalized. Proper capitalization conveys meaning and can change interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: capitalizing common terms ("Sequence", "Limit") for emphasis, or capitalizing a word after a comma when not starting a new sentence. Distinguish common vs proper nouns and avoid ad-hoc capitalization for emphasis. (Coded IC; counts reported by activity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No or Incorrect Punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation gives meaning to written words and functions like pauses/intonation in speech. Incorrect punctuation can change or obscure intended meaning in mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines: write mathematics in complete sentences; punctuate displayed equations when they form part of a sentence; ensure commas, periods, and other punctuation clarify sentence structure. (Coded NIP; examples and counts provided in the study.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague Term or Phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A vague term or phrase is one that is not clear or that suggests different meanings, causing lack of certainty and distinctness in a mathematical statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common instance: overuse of pronouns such as “it” without a clear antecedent ("therefore it converges"—unclear what 'it' refers to). Use specific terminology or explicit mathematical expressions to avoid ambiguity. (Coded VT; tallied across activities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorrect Term or Phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A term or phrase which is not appropriately used in a mathematical statement leading to incorrectness of thought or idea in that statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes: misunderstanding of the mathematical principle or poor choice of words. Check that the chosen terms accurately reflect the underlying mathematical concept; revise wording when it changes the logical content. (Coded IT; examples and frequency discussed.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of Term or Phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to use words or phrases that connect ideas behind mathematical expressions—omitting explanations, definitions, or variable declarations needed for reader comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: presenting only symbolic manipulation without explanatory text; failing to define a variable (e.g., using S_n without stating S is the n-th partial sum). Guidance: supply linking phrases, define variables and notation, and write explanatory sentences so solutions do not 'have to speak for themselves.' (Coded LTP; occurrences were tallied per student output.)
